newsitem.title: FRANCE: France welcomes outcome of Libreville summit.
newsitem.headline: France welcomes outcome of Libreville summit.

text.p: France said on Friday the Libreville Central African summit, at which President Mobutu Sese Seko said he would not seek re-election, had opened the way for the end of civil war and a peaceful transfer of power in Zaire.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said the summit had "opened new prospects for an orderly and peaceful transition, based on the regular functioning of institutions".

Beleaguered and ailing Mobutu, under the threat of a rebel onslaught against Kinshasa, told the presidents of Gabon, Chad, Congo, Central African Republic and Equatorial Guinea he would not run for re-election for health reasons.
The heads of state urged the Kinshasa parliament to fill the vacant post of speaker -- Mobutu's constitutional successor in the event of death or incapacity.

Rummelhardt told a news briefing that Paris had reiterated to visiting U.S. special envoy Bill Richardson that the Zaire crisis could only be solved by a political settlement leading to free elections.

He said Paris backed current diplomatic efforts to end the crisis and was in close touch with United Nations envoy Mohammed Sahnoun and South African authorities who are trying to arrange a fresh meeting between Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
Richardson has said a fresh summit was crucial to ensure a peaceful transfer of power.

Rummelhardt added that Paris had renewed its appeal to some 600 French nationals remaining in Kinshasa to leave. Some 300 French soldiers are among 3,000 troops standing by in Congo, across the river from Kinshasa, to evacuate westerners should the fighting reach the Zaire capital.
The rebels, who control three quarters of the giant, mineral-rich nation and have said they will drive Mobutu from Kinshasa if he does not hand power to Kabila before they arrive in Kinshasa.
